# Glossary {#sec-glossary}

Terms are defined as this book uses them. Where a term has a
broader meaning elsewhere, the definition here is the working
one, and the chapter cross-reference is where it is developed.
Entries are alphabetical within each heading. A term set in bold
in a chapter links to its entry here.

## Reproducibility and compendia

[**Five Pillars.**]{#gloss-five-pillars} The layered stack this
book treats as the minimum for a reproducible project:
Dockerfile, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source code, and data. See
@sec-zzcollab.

[**Methods reproducibility.**]{#gloss-methods-reproducibility}
The property that another analyst, given your code, data, and
environment, obtains your numbers. Distinct from replication,
which asks whether the finding holds in new data. See @sec-why.

[**Provenance.**]{#gloss-provenance} The record of where a data
object came from and what was done to it. A query, a script, and
a dated extraction note are provenance; a file named
`final_v3.csv` is not.

[**Replication.**]{#gloss-replication} Repeating a study with new
data to see whether the finding recurs. A reproducible analysis
can be replicated; an irreproducible one cannot even be checked.
See @sec-why.

[**Research compendium.**]{#gloss-research-compendium} A single
directory holding the code, data, environment specification, and
narrative for one study, organized by convention so that a
stranger can navigate it. See @sec-rrtools.

## Environment and dependencies

[**Apptainer.**]{#gloss-apptainer} A container runtime (formerly
Singularity) used on shared HPC systems, where Docker is usually
unavailable because it requires root. It runs unprivileged and
can build its image from a Docker image. See @sec-cloud-hpc.

[**Docker image.**]{#gloss-docker-image} A built, immutable
filesystem containing an operating system, system libraries, and
R. A container is a running instance of an image. See
@sec-docker.

[**Layer caching.**]{#gloss-layer-caching} Docker's reuse of
unchanged build steps. Slow, stable layers belong early in a
Dockerfile and fast-changing source late, so that editing the
manuscript does not trigger a package reinstall. See @sec-docker.

[**Library path.**]{#gloss-library-path} The ordered list of
directories R searches for installed packages, returned by
`.libPaths()`. R takes the first match and installs into the
first entry. See @sec-workstation.

[**Lockfile.**]{#gloss-lockfile} `renv.lock`, the file recording
every package version a project uses. It is the artifact
committed to version control; the library itself is not. See
@sec-renv.

[**`renv`.**]{#gloss-renv} A package that gives a project its own
library and records exact package versions in a lockfile. See
@sec-renv.

[**`snapshot()` and `restore()`.**]{#gloss-snapshot-restore} The
two halves of the `renv` cycle. `snapshot()` writes the current
library state into the lockfile; `restore()` rebuilds a library
to match a lockfile.

## Version control

[**Branch.**]{#gloss-branch} A named line of development that can
diverge from `main` and later be merged back. See @sec-git-solo.

[**Commit.**]{#gloss-commit} A recorded snapshot of the project
with a message explaining why the change was made. See
@sec-git-solo.

[**Continuous integration (CI).**]{#gloss-continuous-integration}
Automated rebuilding and testing of the project on a fresh
machine at every push, which proves the analysis runs from what
is in the repository rather than from the state of anyone's
laptop. See @sec-ci.

[**Git.**]{#gloss-git} The distributed version-control system
this book uses. It records the project's history as a sequence of
commits, each recoverable, and GitHub hosts a shared copy. See
@sec-git-solo.

[**Merge conflict.**]{#gloss-merge-conflict} The state where two
branches changed the same lines and Git cannot decide which to
keep. Resolved by editing the marked region and committing. See
@sec-git-teams.

[**Pull request.**]{#gloss-pull-request} A proposal to merge a
branch, reviewed by a colleague and checked by CI before it
lands. See @sec-git-teams.

[**Tag.**]{#gloss-tag} A permanent, human-readable name for a
specific commit, used here to mark submission and analysis-plan
versions. See @sec-git-solo-tags.

## Reporting

[**Chunk.**]{#gloss-chunk} A block of executable code in a Quarto
or R Markdown document. A fenced block without braces is
displayed but not executed. See @sec-quarto.

[**Cross-reference.**]{#gloss-cross-reference} A link such as
`@fig-name` that resolves to a numbered figure, table, or
section. An unresolved cross-reference is a build warning, not a
silent failure.

[**Float.**]{#gloss-float} A figure or table that LaTeX may move
away from where it is declared, to avoid awkward white space and
bad page breaks. See @sec-rmd-workflow-floats.

[**`freeze`.**]{#gloss-freeze} A Quarto setting that caches
computed output and re-executes only when the source changes.
See @sec-quarto-freeze.

[**Parameterized report.**]{#gloss-parameterized-report} A
document taking parameters at render time, so that one source
produces a report per cohort or site. See @sec-quarto-params.

[**Quarto.**]{#gloss-quarto} The publishing system this book uses
to weave prose and executed code into HTML, PDF, and Word
documents, websites, and books. The successor to R Markdown. See
@sec-quarto.

[**`spin` and `purl`.**]{#gloss-spin-purl} Complementary `knitr`
functions. `spin()` turns an annotated R script into a document;
`purl()` extracts the code from a document back into a script.
See @sec-rmd-workflow.

## Data wrangling

[**Anti-join audit.**]{#gloss-anti-join-audit} Using
`anti_join()` to list the rows that failed to match, as a check
on a join rather than a step in the pipeline. See @sec-joins.

[**Byte-order mark (BOM).**]{#gloss-byte-order-mark} Invisible
bytes at the start of a text file marking its encoding. Whether
it survives into the first column's name depends on the reader
and the locale, so a script can work on a laptop and fail in a
container. See @sec-acquisition-pathologies.

[**Factor.**]{#gloss-factor} R's type for a categorical variable,
storing a fixed set of levels. Character is the safer type
through reading, cleaning, and joining; factor is correct at
modeling and plotting. See @sec-types.

[**Join.**]{#gloss-join} Combining tables on a key. `inner_join`
keeps matched rows only; `left_join` keeps all rows of the left
table; `full_join` keeps all rows of both. `semi_join` and
`anti_join` filter the left table by presence in the right
without adding columns. See @sec-joins.

[**Key.**]{#gloss-key} The column or columns identifying a row
uniquely in a table. Verifying key uniqueness before a join is
the single most useful check in this book. See @sec-joins.

[**Level and reference level.**]{#gloss-reference-level} The
permitted values of a factor, and the one against which model
coefficients are contrasted. The reference level should be
chosen deliberately, not inherited from alphabetical order. See
@sec-types.

[**Long and wide format.**]{#gloss-long-wide-format} Wide holds
one row per subject with repeated measures across columns; long
holds one row per subject-visit. Plotting and mixed models
generally want long; within-subject differences are easier wide.
See @sec-wrangling.

[**Many-to-many relationship.**]{#gloss-many-to-many} A join in
which the key repeats on both sides, producing the product of the
matches. Usually a key error rather than an intention, which is
why dplyr warns. See @sec-joins.

[**Pipe.**]{#gloss-pipe} An operator that passes the result of one
step to the next, so a transformation reads left to right. R's
native pipe `|>` sends the value on its left as the first
argument of the function on its right; the shell's `|` sends one
command's output to the next command's input. See
@sec-shell-pipes.

[**Pivot.**]{#gloss-pivot} The reshaping operation between long
and wide format, `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`. See
@sec-wrangling-shapes.

[**Tidy data.**]{#gloss-tidy-data} A layout in which each variable
is a column, each observation a row, and each type of
observational unit a table. See @sec-wrangling.

[**Tidy evaluation.**]{#gloss-tidy-evaluation} The mechanism
letting a function accept a bare column name. `{{ col }}`
embraces an argument; `.data[[name]]` takes a column name as a
string. See @sec-wrangling.

## Missing data

[**Complete-case analysis.**]{#gloss-complete-case-analysis}
Dropping rows with any missing value in the model variables. Its
regression coefficients are unbiased when missingness does not
depend on the outcome given the covariates, whatever the
mechanism label, and it always discards information. See
@sec-missing-complete-case.

[**Delta adjustment.**]{#gloss-delta-adjustment} A sensitivity
analysis shifting imputed values by a stated amount to probe
departures from MAR. See @sec-missing-trials.

[**Fraction of missing information (FMI).**]{#gloss-fmi} The share
of the variance of an estimate attributable to missingness,
reported alongside pooled results.

[**Last observation carried forward (LOCF).**]{#gloss-locf} Single
imputation that holds a dropout at the last observed value. The
assumption is biologically implausible for most diseases, and
this book treats it as an antipattern. See @sec-missing-single.

[**MCAR, MAR, MNAR.**]{#gloss-mcar-mar-mnar} Missing completely at
random, missing at random given observed variables, and missing
not at random. The third cannot be tested from the data and
requires sensitivity analysis. See @sec-missing-mechanisms.

[**Mean imputation.**]{#gloss-mean-imputation} Replacing missing
values with the column mean. It understates the spread of the
filled variable and can bias coefficients, and this book treats
it as an antipattern. See @sec-missing-single.

[**MMRM.**]{#gloss-mmrm} Mixed model for repeated measures: a
likelihood analysis of all observed visits with an unstructured
covariance across visits. It imputes nothing and is valid under
MAR; the standard primary analysis for a repeated continuous
outcome in a trial. See @sec-missing-trials.

[**Multiple imputation.**]{#gloss-multiple-imputation} Generating
several completed datasets, fitting the model in each, and
pooling. The between-dataset variation is the uncertainty single
imputation discards. See @sec-missing-mi.

[**Rubin's rules.**]{#gloss-rubins-rules} The formulas combining
within- and between-imputation variance into one standard error.
See @sec-missing-mi.

[**Tipping-point analysis.**]{#gloss-tipping-point-analysis} A
sensitivity analysis that increases a delta adjustment until the
conclusion changes, and asks whether that departure from MAR is
clinically plausible. With a shift per arm, the tipping point is
a boundary in two dimensions. See @sec-missing-trials.

## Trials and analysis plans

[**Analysis set.**]{#gloss-analysis-set} The subjects an analysis
includes, such as the intention-to-treat (full analysis) set or
the per-protocol set. Pre-specified in the SAP and implemented as
ADSL flags. See @sec-cdisc-adam.

[**CONSORT.**]{#gloss-consort} Consolidated Standards of Reporting
Trials, the reporting guideline for randomized trials. Its flow
diagram reports every exclusion and loss with a count. See
@sec-missing-further.

[**Data lock and unblinding.**]{#gloss-data-lock} The point after
which the dataset does not change and treatment assignment
becomes known. Everything pre-specified before it carries the
study's inferential authority. See @sec-analysis-plan.

[**Estimand.**]{#gloss-estimand} A precise statement of what is
being estimated, given by the five ICH E9(R1) attributes:
population, treatment conditions, variable, intercurrent events
with their strategies, and population-level summary. See
@sec-analysis-plan-estimands.

[**Intercurrent event.**]{#gloss-intercurrent-event} An event
after treatment starts that changes the interpretation or the
existence of the outcome, such as nonadherence or death. Each
needs a stated strategy (treatment policy, composite,
hypothetical, while on treatment, or principal stratum). See
@sec-analysis-plan-estimands.

[**Minimum clinically important difference
(MCID).**]{#gloss-mcid} The smallest effect that would matter to
patients or clinicians, fixed in the SAP. An interval is read
against both zero and the MCID to say what it rules out. See
@sec-communicating-null.

[**SAP.**]{#gloss-sap} Statistical analysis plan. Drafted without
data access, tagged in version control, and amended only with a
dated new version. See @sec-analysis-plan.

## Clinical data standards

[**ADaM.**]{#gloss-adam} Analysis Data Model, the analysis-ready
layer the statistician builds from SDTM, each value traceable
back to it. See @sec-cdisc-adam.

[**ADSL, ADTTE, ADAE.**]{#gloss-adsl} The subject-level,
time-to-event, and adverse-event ADaM datasets. See
@sec-cdisc-worked.

[**CRF.**]{#gloss-crf} Case report form, the instrument by which
site staff record data. See @sec-cdisc.

[**Define-XML, aCRF, SDRG, ADRG.**]{#gloss-define-xml} The
metadata and documentation accompanying a submission: the
machine-readable data definition, the annotated CRF, and the
study and analysis data reviewer's guides.

[**Domain.**]{#gloss-domain} An SDTM dataset on one topic, such as
`DM` (demographics), `AE` (adverse events), or `LB` (laboratory
results). See @sec-cdisc-sdtm.

[**Double programming.**]{#gloss-double-programming} Industry's
standard validation: a second programmer derives the same output
independently from the specification, and the two are compared
value by value. See @sec-cdisc-industry.

[**Pharmaverse.**]{#gloss-pharmaverse} A cross-company collection
of R packages for the clinical reporting pipeline, among them
`admiral`, `metacore`, `metatools`, and `xportr`. See
@sec-cdisc-industry.

[**SDTM.**]{#gloss-sdtm} Study Data Tabulation Model, the CDISC
standard for collected data, one row per observation. Immutable
once locked; the statistician reads it and does not edit it. See
@sec-cdisc-sdtm.

[**TLF.**]{#gloss-tlf} Tables, listings, and figures: the outputs
of the statistical analysis, assembled into the clinical study
report. See @sec-cdisc-industry.

[**Transport file (XPT).**]{#gloss-transport-file} The SAS
transport format, version 5, required for regulatory submission
and the durable interchange format between R and SAS. Each
crossing can truncate variable names and lose labels, so each
deserves a check. See @sec-sas.

## Prediction and inference

[**AUC.**]{#gloss-auc} Area under the receiver operating
characteristic curve: the probability that a randomly chosen
case receives a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen
non-case. A measure of discrimination, reported with an interval.
See @sec-adni-model.

[**Cross-validation.**]{#gloss-cross-validation} Estimating
out-of-sample performance by repeatedly fitting on part of the
data and evaluating on the held-out rest. When a participant
contributes several rows, folds must be assigned by participant.
See @sec-adni-model.

[**Data leakage.**]{#gloss-data-leakage} Information from the
evaluation data reaching the model during fitting, for example
the same participant in training and test folds. It makes
performance look better than any new data will confirm. See
@sec-adni-model.

[**MCI.**]{#gloss-mci} Mild cognitive impairment, a heterogeneous
state between normal cognition and dementia; the ADNI case study
predicts conversion from MCI to Alzheimer's disease. See
@sec-adni-question.

[**Target trial.**]{#gloss-target-trial} The hypothetical
randomized trial that would answer a causal question. Target-trial
emulation designs an observational analysis to mimic it, above
all by aligning eligibility, assignment, and the start of
follow-up. See @sec-ethics-causal.

## Privacy and data governance

[**Data use agreement (DUA).**]{#gloss-dua} A contract under which
data are received, commonly forbidding re-identification,
contact, and redistribution. Its terms bind even after
de-identification. See @sec-deident-obligations and
@sec-adni-dua.

[**Date shifting.**]{#gloss-date-shifting} Offsetting every date
for a patient by a constant, preserving within-patient intervals
while destroying calendar time. See @sec-deident-transformations.

[**Expert Determination.**]{#gloss-expert-determination} The HIPAA
de-identification method in which a qualified expert certifies,
using accepted methods, that the risk of re-identification is very
small. More flexible than Safe Harbor and more involved. See
@sec-deident-pathways.

[**HIPAA.**]{#gloss-hipaa} The Health Insurance Portability and
Accountability Act. Its Privacy Rule governs protected health
information and defines the de-identification pathways. See
@sec-deident.

[**IRB.**]{#gloss-irb} Institutional review board, the committee
that approves and oversees research with human subjects. Its
protocol, with any DUA, decides whether an analysis may start.
See @sec-team-science-intake.

[**k-anonymity.**]{#gloss-k-anonymity} The property that every
combination of quasi-identifier values in a dataset is shared by
at least $k$ records. Achieved by generalizing and suppressing;
refinements such as l-diversity address weaknesses it leaves.
See @sec-deident-risk.

[**Limited data set.**]{#gloss-limited-data-set} Data with the
direct identifiers removed but dates, city, state, and ZIP code
kept. It is still PHI and may be disclosed for research only
under a DUA. See @sec-deident-pathways.

[**PHI.**]{#gloss-phi} Protected health information: individually
identifiable health information held by a covered entity, as
defined by the HIPAA Privacy Rule. See @sec-deident.

[**Quasi-identifier.**]{#gloss-quasi-identifier} A field that is
not an identifier alone but becomes one in combination, such as
ZIP code with date of birth and sex. See @sec-deident.

[**Safe Harbor.**]{#gloss-safe-harbor} The HIPAA de-identification
method that removes eighteen specified categories of identifier,
with no actual knowledge that the rest could identify anyone. The
result is de-identified, not anonymous. See @sec-deident-pathways.

## Research ethics

[**Aggregation harm.**]{#gloss-aggregation-harm} Harm from
assembling individually innocuous disclosures into a whole that
exposes people, the ethical counterpart of quasi-identifiers. See
@sec-ethics-aggregation.

[**HARKing.**]{#gloss-harking} Hypothesizing after the results are
known: presenting a hypothesis formed from the data as if it had
been stated in advance. A questionable research practice that a
tagged analysis plan prevents. See @sec-ethics-standards.

[**Overlapping-interval
fallacy.**]{#gloss-overlapping-interval-fallacy} Concluding that
two groups do not differ because their confidence intervals
overlap. The interval for the difference is narrower than the
two intervals suggest and can exclude zero. See
@sec-ethics-overlap.

[**Questionable research practices
(QRPs).**]{#gloss-questionable-research-practices} Practices
between misconduct and good practice, such as HARKing,
undisclosed analytic flexibility, and selective reporting. Rarely
fraud and frequently decisive. See @sec-ethics-standards.

[**Research misconduct.**]{#gloss-research-misconduct} Under the
federal definition, fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in
proposing, performing, reviewing, or reporting research.
Omitting data without disclosure is falsification. See
@sec-ethics-standards.

## Testing

[**End-to-end test.**]{#gloss-end-to-end-test} A test running raw
data through to final outputs. Slow, broad, and the last line of
defense.

[**Integration test.**]{#gloss-integration-test} A test running
the whole pipeline on a small synthetic dataset. Catches
composition bugs and silent filter and join errors, and has the
best cost-benefit ratio for analysis code.

[**Mutation testing.**]{#gloss-mutation-testing} Planting
deliberate bugs (mutants) to see whether the test suite fails on
them. The share of mutants killed measures how much the suite can
see. See @sec-testing-worked.

[**Snapshot test.**]{#gloss-snapshot-test} A test comparing output
against a recorded version, which detects change without
asserting correctness.

[**Structural versus correctness
assertion.**]{#gloss-structural-correctness-assertion} Checking
that a result has the right shape, against checking that it holds
the right values. Only the second is a correctness test. See
@sec-testing-correctness.

[**Tautological test.**]{#gloss-tautological-test} A test that
passes regardless of whether the code is right, such as comparing
a function's output to itself. See @sec-testing-smells.

[**Unit test.**]{#gloss-unit-test} A test of one function on known
input. Fast, narrow, and catches helper bugs. See @sec-testing.

## AI-assisted coding

[**Prompt injection.**]{#gloss-prompt-injection} Text in a file,
web page, or README that an agent reads, written to instruct the
model. The agent cannot reliably tell it from your instructions,
so what it reads is untrusted. See @sec-ai-governance.

[**Slopsquatting.**]{#gloss-slopsquatting} Registering a package
name that models hallucinate, with malicious code, so that an
unchecked install runs it. Confirm a package exists before
installing it. See @sec-ai-governance.

## Graphics

[**Aesthetic mapping.**]{#gloss-aesthetic-mapping} The assignment
of a variable to a visual property such as position, color, or
shape. The grammar of graphics requires the variable to be a
column, which is why plotting usually wants long format. See
@sec-graphics.

[**Alt text.**]{#gloss-alt-text} A short description of what a
figure shows, read by screen readers. Required for informative
images; decorative images take an empty description instead.

[**Faceting.**]{#gloss-faceting} Splitting one plot into small
multiples by a grouping variable. See @sec-graphics.

[**Truncated axis.**]{#gloss-truncated-axis} A y-axis not
beginning at zero, which exaggerates a difference without
containing a false number. See @sec-ethics-visual.

## Pipelines

[**DAG.**]{#gloss-dag} Directed acyclic graph. In a pipeline, the
dependency structure: editing one node makes everything
downstream stale and nothing upstream (@sec-targets-dag). In
causal inference, a diagram of assumed causal structure from
which an adjustment set is read (@sec-ethics-causal).

[**Makefile.**]{#gloss-makefile} The file read by `make`, listing
named targets and the commands that build them. A `zzcollab`
project's `Makefile` wraps the routine Docker and render
commands. See @sec-zzcollab-optional.

[**Target.**]{#gloss-target} One node of a `targets` pipeline: a
named object with declared dependencies, rebuilt only when those
change. See @sec-targets.

## Open publishing

[**CC BY.**]{#gloss-cc-by} The Creative Commons Attribution
license, permitting adaptation and commercial use with credit.
The standard recommendation for open textbooks.

[**dbGaP.**]{#gloss-dbgap} The NIH Database of Genotypes and
Phenotypes, a controlled-access repository for studies that pair
genotype with phenotype. The wrong home for general clinical
data. See @sec-federal-repository.

[**Deposition.**]{#gloss-deposition} Placing data or code in a
repository that guarantees persistence, as distinct from hosting
it on a personal page or a lab server. See @sec-federal.

[**DMSP.**]{#gloss-dmsp} Data Management and Sharing Plan, required
by NIH with each application that will generate scientific data
and approved as a term of the award. It states what will be
shared, where, and when. See @sec-federal-dmsp.

[**DOI.**]{#gloss-doi} Digital object identifier, a permanent
citable handle for a deposited artifact. See @sec-federal.

[**Open educational resource (OER).**]{#gloss-oer} A teaching work
licensed to permit reuse, revision, and redistribution. Licenses
forbidding derivative works do not qualify.
